sections.heading: Stop trying to pay you back with better behavior
sections.text: My Father, when my sin brings your fatherly displeasure, I often try to make things right by promising I will do better next time. Please teach me how wrong that instinct is. My future obedience cannot repair my past disobedience. I cannot satisfy your law by improving myself. When I lean on my own efforts, even my religious efforts, I am quietly trusting my own righteousness instead of yours.
theological_themes: Human effort cannot atone for sin or satisfy God's law.
Self-reform becomes self-righteousness when it is treated as the basis of peace with God.
True repentance begins by giving up confidence in personal merit.

scripture_references.connection: Paul insists that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ. This directly supports the prayer's rejection of trying to restore peace with God by future obedience or moral improvement.

This passage says the law exposes sin rather than providing a way for sinners to be made righteous by their own performance. It grounds the prayer's confession that only God's grace, not self-correction, can answer guilt.

sections.heading: Resting in the finished righteousness of Christ
sections.text: Father, bring me back to what is already complete in Jesus. His righteousness is not something I add to or finish. It is ready, finished, and enough. When you correct me for my sin, do not let me treat that correction as a demand to earn my way back to you. Use it to humble me, grieve me over sin, pull me away from it, and drive me again to Christ, where I am reconciled to you and counted righteous by faith.
theological_themes: Christ's finished righteousness is the believer's only ground of acceptance before God.
God's discipline is not a call to self-atonement but a means of humbling and restoring his child.
Faith receives reconciliation and righteousness in Christ.

scripture_references.connection: Paul contrasts his own righteousness with the righteousness from God that comes through faith in Christ. This supports the prayer's emphasis that only Christ's completed righteousness is fit to stand before God.

Hebrews presents God's discipline as the loving correction of a Father who trains his children in holiness. That clarifies the prayer's claim that chastening is meant to humble and separate from sin, not to make the believer pay for sin.

Paul links justification by faith with peace with God through Jesus Christ. This grounds the prayer's movement from conviction and discipline back into reconciliation through Christ rather than personal achievement.

sections.heading: Depending on you through faith, not depending on faith itself
sections.text: Teach me to stand because Christ is strong, not because I imagine my faith is strong. Any steadiness I have comes from finding my sufficiency in him. I do not want to trust in my faith as though faith itself could hold me up. I want to trust you by faith, because you are my only support. And yet I do not want to despise faith or throw it away, because by faith I take hold of you. Since you are precious to me, the faith that receives you is precious too.
theological_themes: The object of faith is God in Christ, not the believer's own believing.
Faith is precious because it receives and clings to God.
Stability in the Christian life comes from Christ's sufficiency, not self-confidence.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that his disciples can bear fruit only by abiding in him and that apart from him they can do nothing. This supports the prayer's insistence that all spiritual sufficiency and stability come from Christ.

Peter speaks of tested faith as precious because it endures through trials and results in praise to Christ. This helps explain the prayer's careful balance: faith is not the Savior, but it is precious because it holds to him.
Paul calls believers to continue walking in Christ the same way they received him, rooted and built up in him. This supports relying on Christ by faith as the ongoing pattern of the Christian life.

sections.heading: Confessing why I do not pursue holiness as I should
sections.text: Father, I fall short of the purity you call me to. Sometimes I assume I am already holy enough, so I stop seeking holiness. Other times I decide I am too weak to change, so I stop trying at all. Humble me for both sins. Forgive me for not being as holy as I should be, and for not becoming as holy as I could become through Christ's help.
theological_themes: Presumption and despair both hinder growth in holiness.
Believers remain responsible to pursue holiness while depending entirely on Christ's help.
Humility is needed both when seeing sin and when seeking change.

scripture_references.connection: Paul states plainly that God's will for believers is their sanctification. This supports the prayer's confession that holiness is not optional or something to neglect through complacency.

Peter says God has given believers what they need for godliness and then calls them to make every effort to grow. This fits the prayer's concern to reject both self-sufficient pride and passive defeatism.

Paul holds together active obedience and God's inward work in believers. That balance illuminates the prayer's desire to pursue holiness through Christ rather than either boasting in ability or giving up because of weakness.

sections.heading: Let nothing created stand between you and me
sections.text: You are everything, Father, and to have you is to have what I truly need. But whenever I make myself, my performance, my strength, or any created thing into something ultimate, I put it between us. Then I stop walking humbly with you, and I stop walking in holiness. Lord, forgive me for this. Bring me back to simple dependence on you.
theological_themes: God himself is the believer's supreme good and portion.
Created things, including the self, become obstacles when treated as ultimate grounds of confidence.
Humility and holiness grow as the believer depends on God rather than on the creature.

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist confesses that God is his supreme desire and lasting portion even when human strength fails. This supports the prayer's claim that to possess God is to possess all that is truly needed.

Jeremiah contrasts trusting in man and flesh with trusting in the Lord. This directly speaks to the prayer's warning that making the creature into the source of confidence separates the heart from humble reliance on God.

John assures believers that confession is met by God's faithful forgiveness and cleansing. This grounds the closing plea for forgiveness without turning that plea into self-punishment or self-atonement.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original speaks of God being angry toward the believer and chastising for sin. In this adaptation, that was rendered as 'fatherly displeasure' and 'correction' to preserve the seriousness of sin while distinguishing God's fatherly discipline from condemning wrath, since the prayer is addressed to 'My Father' and rests in Christ's righteousness.

The original says God's chastising is 'not that I should try to reform.' This could be misunderstood as opposing sanctification. The adaptation interprets it as rejecting self-reform as satisfaction for sin, not rejecting Spirit-enabled repentance and growth in holiness.

The original's language about faith being 'very precious' could sound as though faith itself is the ground of salvation. The adaptation makes explicit that faith is precious as the means of receiving God in Christ, not as an independent object of trust.
significant_interpretive_choices: 'Christ's righteousness, ready made, already finished' was rendered as Christ's completed righteousness being enough, emphasizing justification by faith rather than a process the believer contributes to.
'A sense of my sufficiency and ability in him' was interpreted as confidence in Christ's sufficiency for stability and holiness, not confidence in the believer's natural ability.

'If I cast away my faith I cast away thee, for by faith I apprehend thee' was rendered as not despising or abandoning faith because faith takes hold of God. This preserves the instrumental role of faith without suggesting faith replaces God.

'To make the creature something' was interpreted broadly as making self, performance, strength, or any created thing ultimate, because the original contrasts creaturely confidence with humble possession of God as all.
